pages.name: Welcome to Essence
pages.content:
Essence is a tabletop game about sharp, tactical combat and roleplay that stays entirely in your hands. When a fight breaks out, you'll manage dice pools, positioning, and a hand of cards that spell out exactly what your character can do. Outside of combat, the rules step back and your table drives the story.

This guide covers how to actually play a session from inside Foundry — your character sheet, rolling dice, and running combat through the tools this system gives you. For the full rules themselves, see the Combat Styles Reference journal and the Essence rulebook.

Three Domains, No Classes

Every character is built from three domains — Physical (Might, Grace, Vigor), Mental (Intellect, Acuity, Resolve), and Spiritual (Presence, Adaptability, Anima). There's no class to pick. Your Attributes, Combat Skills, Species, Heritage, Distinction, and equipment combine into a character that's genuinely yours — two people who both invest in the same Combat Skill can still play completely differently.

Where to Start

New to the sheet? Read Your Character Sheet next, then Combat once you're ready to fight. Everything else can wait until it comes up at the table.

pages.name: Your Character Sheet
pages.content:
Open your character from the Actors sidebar tab. Don't have one yet? Click Create Character, then open the wand icon in the sheet's header to launch the Character Creation Wizard — it walks you through Attributes, Skills, Species/Heritage/Distinction, and starting Equipment step by step.

Your sheet is split into tabs: Core (Attributes, Resources, Wounds), Combat (Action/Reaction Cards, your Combat Style specialty), Equipment, Non-Combat, and Biography. Everything you need in a given moment lives on the relevant tab — you don't need to memorize the whole system, just know where to look.

pages.name: Attributes, Skills & Resources
pages.content:
Your 9 Attributes sit inside the three domains: Physical (Might, Grace, Vigor), Mental (Intellect, Acuity, Resolve), and Spiritual (Presence, Adaptability, Anima). Each domain also has a Resource you spend to act (Stamina, Focus, Mana) and a Defense others roll against to hit you (Fortitude, Composure, Harmony).

Each domain covers three Combat Skills as well. Five of the nine — Gestalt, Magecraft, Psionics, Ritualism, and Calling — are gated: you need the matching Distinction before you can raise them above 0. Your sheet greys these out until you qualify.

pages.name: Rolling Dice
pages.content:
Click a skill's name to roll it. Outside of combat, you'll choose an Attribute to pair it with for a straightforward check.

In combat, rolling a skill or an Action/Reaction Card spends from a pool instead — your Action Dice on your own Turn, your Reaction Dice on everyone else's. You choose how many dice to commit (at least the card's minimum, up to whatever's left in the pool); that many d10s get rolled and deducted from the pool at once.

Your highest die is your Success Die, compared against the target's Defense to see if you hit. Every other die that shows 6 or higher generates a Surge, which you spend on the bonus options printed on the card — extra damage, more range, and so on. More dice means better odds and more Surges, but fewer dice left for whatever happens next.

pages.name: Wounds & Recovery
pages.content:
Essence doesn't use a hit point bar. Damage moves through three steps:

It first piles up against your Resilience, a buffer that resets at the start of each of your Turns. Once damage exceeds that buffer, you take a real Wound — a Temporary Wound if you have one available, otherwise a Core Wound. You have 5 Core Wound boxes, filled in order: 2 Light, 2 Serious, then 1 Critical.

Your Wound State (Unharmed / Lightly / Seriously / Critically Wounded) depends only on how many Core Wound boxes are filled — not on any single hit. If you fill that last Critical box, the Death Track starts advancing at the start of each of your Turns until it's stabilized or reaches its end.

pages.name: Combat
pages.content:
Combat runs through Foundry's own Combat Tracker (the crossed-swords tab in the sidebar). When the GM starts an encounter, click your sheet's Roll Initiative button (the tracker's own dice icon next to your name does the same thing) and choose how many dice to commit: 0 passes, and whatever you hold back carries over as extra Action Dice on your first Turn.

On your Turn, spend Action Dice on cards and skills. At the end of it, click End Turn to convert whatever's left into Reaction Dice you can use on other players' Turns. Burn Dice lets you spend dice straight from a pool without rolling, for costs that call for it — clearing a Condition, paying a Rite's Echo, and so on.

pages.name: Combat Style Specialties
pages.content:
Every Combat Skill comes with its own resource to track — Combo for Prowess, Lock for Ballistics, Threads for Magecraft, and so on through all nine. Your sheet's Combat tab shows the tracker for whichever specialty applies to you.

See the Combat Styles Reference journal for the full rules on each one, including its Expertises and card subtypes. If you're playing a Calling character who's reached Full Manifestation, see the separate Full Manifestation Guide journal.

pages.name: Setting Up NPCs
pages.content:
Create an NPC the same way as a Character — from the Actors sidebar's Create Actor button, with Type set to NPC / Adversary. NPCs use the exact same Attributes, Skills, Resources, Wounds, and Combat Dice as player characters; they just skip the player-facing fields (Concept, Career, Non-Combat Skills) in favor of a Role tag (Minion/Standard/Elite/Nemesis) and a GM Notes field for tactics reminders.

Leave NPC tokens unlinked (Foundry's default) so multiple copies of the same monster track their own Wounds independently. Character tokens are force-linked instead, since a PC should always be the same Actor everywhere.

Portrait Art vs. Token Art

Every Actor has two separate images: the sheet Portrait (click the art in the header) and the canvas Token Image. Foundry copies your Portrait into the Token Image automatically the first time you set one — after that, the two are independent, so changing one later never touches the other. Use the small pawn icon on the Portrait's corner to set the Token Image directly. Since NPC tokens are unlinked, updating an NPC's Token Image only affects tokens you place after the change; drag a fresh one from the sheet, or right-click a placed token → Configure Token to update it individually.

pages.name: Running Combat
pages.content:
Combat runs entirely through Foundry's own Combat Tracker — add combatants, click Begin Combat, and advance rounds and turns from there. Every way of rolling Initiative (the tracker's dice icon, its Roll All/Roll NPCs buttons, or a sheet's own button) opens the same dice-commit prompt and works identically, so it doesn't matter which one anyone uses.

Ending the encounter (deleting the Combat) automatically resets each combatant's combat state and clears anything — Threads, Authority, and so on — that's meant to expire at the Encounter's end.

pages.name: Conditions & Content
pages.content:
Conditions live in the Conditions compendium and double as Token HUD status icons — right-click a token, open its status-effects palette, and toggle a Condition directly. This adds or removes a real owned Condition item on the Actor, with whatever mechanical effect the rules define (Chilled's Movement penalty, for instance), exactly the same as dragging the Condition onto the sheet by hand.

Authoring New Content

If you have Foundry's "Create Items" permission, a wand-icon scene-control button opens the Create Content wizard for building new Action/Reaction Cards, Equipment, and Conditions straight into the compendium — no hand-editing the data model required. For adding many at once, use its Bulk Import option: download a CSV template, fill it out, and upload it to create or update several items in one pass.

Compendiums

Species, Heritages, and Distinctions are hand-authored. The Combat Styles Reference and Full Manifestation Guide journals document their respective mechanics in full. See the system's README if you need to know where a given compendium's content actually comes from.

pages.name: Role Budget System
pages.content:
Every NPC carries a Role tag — Minion, Standard, Elite, or Nemesis. The Monster Creator's Auto-Generate Stat Block button uses a tunable budget table (four Roles, seven axes each) to fill one out for you in seconds, then hands every result back for you to hand-edit like anything else on the sheet.

RoleAttributesSkillsResilienceTemp WoundsCards (A/R)Equipment
Minion2 pts, max 22 pts, max 21 + 1×Tier01 / 01
Standard7 pts, max 35 pts, max 33 + 2×Tier12 / 12
Elite10 pts, max 48 pts, max 45 + 3×Tier23 / 23
Nemesis13 pts, max 512 pts, max 57 + 4×Tier34 / 34

Auto-Generate rolls, in order: a weighted Attribute/Skill point-buy (leaning toward whichever domain you pick as Emphasis, respecting the same five Distinction gates a player would), Resilience/Temp Wounds/Equipment Limit straight from the table above, a set of qualifying Combat Cards weighted toward the Skills that rolled highest, and a random Equipment draw. Each step has its own Reroll button if you just want to redo one part.

Treat this table as a starting point, not a law — every number lives in module/data/monster-budgets.mjs and takes effect immediately if you tune it.

pages.name: What Full Manifestation Is
pages.content:
Calling represents a bond between your character and a supernatural entity — a spirit, ancestor, or other manifested power. Most Calling cards channel only a piece of that bond: a claw, a shielding wing, a borrowed sense. You stay in play, playing yourself.

Full Manifestation is different. At greater commitment, your character steps aside and the entity takes their place on the battlefield — using its own combat profile, its own Actions and Reactions, and its own Wound Track. You aren't gaining a second creature standing next to you; you disappear, and it stands where you were.

Eight manifestations are available, gated by your Calling Rank: Familiar or Sprite at Rank 0; add Beast, Phantom, or Golem at Rank 1; add Elemental, Ancestor, or Fey at Rank 2. See The Eight Profiles for each one's stat block.

pages.name: Entering a Full Manifestation
pages.content:
Play an eligible Calling Action as normal and pay its printed cost. If it hits — or resolves however it resolves — you may then pay an additional toll to fully manifest: burn 3 more Action Dice (2 if you have the Summoner Origin) plus Mana equal to the card's Rank + 1. Dice you already rolled for the card can't also pay this burn, and a Reaction can never trigger a Full Manifestation.

Once you've paid it, open your sheet's header menu (the ⋮ icon, top right) and choose Full Manifestation. Pick the subtype that card's Rider names. Your token immediately swaps to that manifestation's own sheet and stat block for the rest of the Encounter.

The first subtype you manifest into during a fight is locked in for that entire fight — you can dismiss and re-enter that same body as many times as you like, but you can't switch to a different one until the Encounter ends.

pages.name: While You're Manifested
pages.content:
You aren't getting a fresh turn. The manifestation picks up exactly where you left off: whatever Action Dice and Reaction Dice you had left are all it has, and any Movement you'd already spent this Turn stays spent. Your own Wounds and Conditions are all still true underneath — manifesting heals nothing.

Your card options shrink to match: only that profile's own 2-3 built-in maneuvers, plus universal Basics like Hide or Strike. Your learned catalogue — every card from every Style you know — is off the table until you return to your own body. Your normal weapon and armor sit out of play too; they add nothing to a profile's own attacks.

To leave voluntarily, open the manifestation's own header menu and choose Return to [Your Name] — this costs 1 Action Die, burned on your Turn. You return to the space you left, and can't manifest again until you play another eligible Calling card.

pages.name: Damage, Wounds & Defeat
pages.content:
Each profile has its own Wound Track (3 to 5 boxes, depending on the subtype), completely separate from your own 5 Core Wounds. It's also persistent — because your manifestation lives in Foundry as your own dedicated NPC Actor, any Wounds it takes are still there the next time you manifest that same subtype, even in a later session.

The damage pressure building toward your next Wound (your Resilience buffer) belongs to you, not to whichever body is currently active. It doesn't reset just because you transformed, dismissed, or were knocked out of a manifestation — so switching bodies can't be used to shrug off a hit that's already landed, and you'll never be charged twice for the same one.

Example: you'd already taken 2 points of unresolved damage before manifesting your Golem (Resilience 2). Manifesting itself costs you nothing. A hit for 1 more damage now pushes your total to 3 — 1 point over Resilience — so the Golem takes exactly 1 Wound. If you'd manifested at 0 pressure instead, that same hit wouldn't have caused a Wound at all.

Defeat

If a hit fills a manifestation's last Wound box, it collapses immediately: you're forced back into your own body, you take 1 automatic Wound from the shock, and any part of that hit's damage that didn't fit on the manifestation's track transfers to you as well (Temporary Wounds can absorb either). That specific subtype is marked Broken until Downtime — your other seven remain available. On the manifestation's own sheet, a GM or the player resolves this with the Apply Manifestation Defeat header menu option once its Wound Track is full.

pages.name: The Eight Profiles
pages.content:
SubtypeRankBodyFortitudeComposureHarmonyResilienceMovementWound Capacity
Familiar0Living566043
Sprite0Living566043
Beast1Living756144
Phantom1Nonliving677034
Golem1Nonliving765224
Elemental2Nonliving778135
Ancestor2Nonliving878135

A profile marked Living is a valid target for a living-only effect; one marked Nonliving is not — but it still feels pain, can be restrained, and is affected by mental attacks, magic, and ordinary Conditions like anything else. Being a Phantom doesn't make you incorporeal.

Open any profile directly from the Calling Full Manifestations compendium to read its full stat block and maneuvers, exactly like any other NPC.

pages.name: For Game Masters
pages.content:
The first time a character fully manifests a given subtype, the system automatically creates that character's own persistent copy of the profile and hands the controlling player Owner permission on it — you don't need to drag anything from the compendium yourself. Every later manifestation of the same subtype reuses that same copy, which is what makes its Wound Track actually persist between sessions.

Entering, dismissing, and resolving a defeat are all one click from a sheet's own header menu — the character's token swaps to the manifestation for the duration and swaps back automatically. The only things still tracked by hand are the same ones every other Combat Style Specialty already is: paying the entry cost, and clicking Apply Manifestation Defeat once a Wound Track fills.
